display.title: Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD) method
display.summary: An extension of Selective Synaptic Dampening that replaces Fisher-information parameter importance with the gradient of the squared l2 norm of the model output, removing the need for loss or ground-truth labels.

display.title: Retraining- and label-free unlearning needing only unlabelled forget samples
display.summary: The first retraining-free unlearning method that requires only unlabelled forget-set inputs at forgetting time, without long-term storage of the retain set, labels, or forget-set loss.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: In the ViT subclass rows of Table 6, LFSSD's forget-set accuracy diverges from both SSD and the retrained model. On one row it is 31.42 versus SSD's 6.68. On another, its MIA score is 1.60 versus 77.37 for the retrained model. These gaps contradict a blanket equivalence claim. In addition, hyperparameter alpha was chosen per task, with SSD and LFSSD using different values. No timing table appears in the paper. The complexity argument alone supports the claim at the level of asymptotic cost. The compute-time claim is not quantified in the inspected text. In addition, SSD's hyperparameters were tuned with Optuna while LFSSD's were tuned with a simplified search, so the comparison is not controlled.
points: Across most tables, LFSSD's results track SSD and the retrained model. However, the claim that it is 'equally effective' is broader than the subclass results support.
The claim of similar compute time to SSD is asserted, but no timing measurements are reported.
Both the 'equally effective as Fisher' claim and the 'similar compute time' claim rest on informal assertion. No timing data or controlled head-to-head ablation is reported.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: The authors credit both components to prior work. They claim novelty only for the transfer into unlearning, which is a modest but clearly positioned increment. Whether the estimator has truly never been used in unlearning is author-reported and was not verified here. The authors themselves position the work as a combination of two cited components (SSD and the Aljundi et al. estimator). The novelty is therefore the transfer and its label-free consequence. Neither the prior work nor the claim that the estimator has not been applied in unlearning was independently verified.
points: The method combines two existing components: SSD's dampening rule and the Memory Aware Synapses sensitivity estimator. The paper states this provenance openly. The novelty lies in this combination and in applying it to unlearning.

The authors frame the originality as a transfer: the importance estimator comes from continual learning, and the claimed novelty is applying it to unlearning. They do not claim to have invented the estimator.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

significance.reasoning: Unlearning without labels and without retraining widens the range of deployment settings. This makes the work likely useful to practitioners and to researchers building on SSD. However, the impact claims ('more practically useful') rest on argument rather than experiments in these settings. The authors name concrete settings where labels are unavailable, such as a catalogue of copyrighted data or semi-supervised models. In those settings, Fisher-based SSD cannot run.
points: Removing the label requirement has plausible practical utility. The paper names copyright catalogues and semi-supervised models as use cases, but neither scenario is evaluated.
Removing the label requirement extends SSD-style unlearning to practical scenarios that the authors motivate.

originality.reasoning: The method still requires full-dataset importance values, computed once over D. Its 'only' claim therefore holds at forgetting time, not overall. The paper also cites zero-shot unlearning work (Chundawat 2023b) without stating how LFSSD differs from it on data requirements.
points: The primacy claim of being 'first retraining-free method requiring only unlabelled forget samples' is hedged with 'to the best of our knowledge'. However, the related-work discussion in this paper is brief, and the claim needs sharper scoping.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: In the Table 6 'sea' rows, retrain keeps Df accuracy at about 91-95%, while LFSSD drops it to about 18-21%. The authors themselves flag this kind of over-forgetting as harmful, via the Streisand effect.
points: LFSSD's results are broadly close to SSD and retrain, but it is not uniformly 'similar to retrain'. In several Cifar20 subclass cases, forget accuracy diverges markedly from retrain.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: Reusing established protocols makes the results comparable with prior work, but the evaluation design is not an original contribution.
points: The empirical-evaluation contribution follows existing benchmark protocols, so it is not novel in itself. It serves as validation of the method.

ABSTRACT
